content: Iodine-129 (129I) is a radioactive isotope of iodine. It undergoes radioactive decay with a half-life of approximately 15.7 million years, emitting low-energy beta particles and gamma radiation during its decay process, ultimately transforming into xenon-129 (129Xe). Among all fission products, 129I has the longest half-life, making it one of only seven fission products classified as long-lived. The fission yield of iodine-129 is approximately 0.6576% per fission event. This yield is about 10% of the production rate of other notable fission products such as technetium-99 (Tc-99), zirconium-93 (Zr-93), or cesium-135 (Cs-135). However, it is significantly higher than the yields of palladium-107 (Pd-107), selenium-79 (Se-79), or tin-126 (Sn-126). While larger quantities of heavier iodine isotopes, such as iodine-131 (131I), are generated during fission, these isotopes have much shorter half-lives. As a result, the iodine content in cooled spent nuclear fuel predominantly consists of approximately 5/6 iodine-129 and 1/6 iodine-127, the latter being the only stable isotope of iodine. Due to its long half-life, iodine-129 poses challenges for environmental containment. It is relatively difficult to immobilize in the environment and has a modest but adequate neutron absorption cross-section. Additionally, it is not significantly diluted by other isotopes of iodine, making it a prime candidate for nuclear transmutation. Along with technetium-99, iodine-129 is considered one of the leading fission products for disposal through re-irradiation with neutrons. This process aims to transmute these isotopes into more stable or shorter-lived forms. In contrast, actinide wastes, which are not fission products, are better suited for disposal through fission in advanced reactor systems such as fast reactors, accelerator-driven subcritical reactors, or fusion-fission hybrid reactors.
